title: Design menu search
dek: Someone in Pune types "panir butter masala" and expects the right dish from restaurants that are open and deliver to them, in a blink. Search 3 crore dishes across India by their words, cope with Hinglish spellings, and show a price change within a minute.

items: Don't scan dishes for the words. Build an inverted index: for each word, the list of dishes that contain it. A search reads a few short lists and combines them.
Clean the query first: fix spellings, map Hinglish and synonyms ("panir", "panner" → paneer; "makhani" ↔ butter), and use the same rules when indexing.
Split the index by city, and within a big city into a few shards. A search asks every shard of its city at once and merges their best results.
Rank by how well the words match, then adjust for what matters here: open now, delivers to you, distance, how popular the dish is, what you've ordered before.
Menu changes reach the index within a minute. Things that change constantly, like "sold out", are kept in a small fast layer checked at search time instead of re-indexing.
Search dishes and restaurants by words, in English and Hinglish, with typos.
Filters: veg only, price range, open now, delivers to me.
Results ranked so the dish you meant is near the top; the first page in well under 200 ms.
Out of scope here: suggestions while typing (see the autocomplete question) and ads in results.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: Results in under 200 ms, even at dinner
A price or menu change searchable within a minute; sold out within seconds
The dish people meant is in the first few results
3 crore dishes, about 1,000 searches a second at dinner

items: Dishes: 3 lakh restaurants × about 100 dishes is 3 crore dishes. At about 300 bytes of text each, 9 GB of text; the index is of a similar size.
Searches: 1 crore people × 2 searches a day is 2 crore a day, about 230 a second on average and around 1,000 at dinner.
Changes: prices, new dishes, items going out of stock: say 50 lakh changes a day, about 60 a second, with spikes when restaurants open.
Per city: a big city like Pune has maybe 15,000 restaurants and 15 lakh dishes; a few shards with copies handle its searches easily.
Dish document (in the index): `dish_id`, `restaurant_id`, `city`, `name`, `description`, `words` (after cleaning), `veg`, `price`, `popularity`.
Restaurant info used at search time: `open_now`, `delivery_area`, `location`, `rating`.
Fast layer: per dish, `sold_out` and per restaurant `busy`, updated in seconds.

body.label: API
body.say: Search a city with words, filters and where you are. The answer says how the query was corrected.

body.cap: The query service fixes spelling and adds synonyms, asks every shard of the city's index at once, merges their best 20 and re-ranks for this person. Menu changes reach the shards through an indexer within a minute.

body.x: The menus database stays the truth; the index is a copy built for searching and can always be rebuilt from it. Searches never touch the menus database.

body.name: First try
body.what: Search the dishes table with WHERE name LIKE '%paneer%' AND name LIKE '%butter%'.
body.use: Works on a test database with a few thousand dishes.
body.avoid: A pattern with a leading % can't use an index, so every search reads every dish in the city. It also can't fix "panir" or rank the best match first.
body.ex: At 8 pm, 1,000 searches a second each read 15 lakh Pune dishes; the menus database is buried.
body.like: Reading every page of every menu in the city to find the word paneer.

body.name: Better
body.what: When a dish is added, split its text into cleaned words and add the dish to each word's list. A search looks up its words' lists and combines them: dishes in all lists first, then dishes in most.
body.use: Each search reads a few short lists, not every dish; the lists also tell how well a dish matches, for ranking.
body.avoid: Very common words ("chicken", "masala") have long lists; read them in ranked order and stop once the top results are clear. Search engines like Elasticsearch or OpenSearch do this for you.
body.ex: "paneer butter masala" reads three lists and puts Paneer Butter Masala first, Paneer Masala Dosa second.
body.like: The index at the back of a book: look up a word, get the pages.

body.cap: Each word points to the dishes that contain it. "paneer butter masala" combines three short lists: d12 has all three words and ranks first, d40 has two, d55 one.

items: Clean words the same way at index time and at search time: lower case, remove punctuation, reduce plurals ("momos" → momo).
A list of spellings and synonyms built from real searches: panir, panner → paneer; makhani ↔ butter; biriyani → biryani; dahi ↔ curd.
For words not in the list, allow one wrong letter in words of five letters or more, and show "showing results for paneer" so the person knows.
Text match first: dishes with all the words, with rarer words counting more ("makhani" matters more than "masala").
Then what makes a result useful here: open now and delivers to you (filter out the rest), distance or delivery time, how often this dish is ordered, the restaurant's rating.
Personal touch last, on the merged top results only: dishes and restaurants this person has ordered before move up.
Menu changes are written to the menus database and to a change log. The indexer reads the log and updates the index in small batches every second or so; changes are searchable within a minute.
"Sold out" and "restaurant busy" change many times an evening. Keep them in a small in-memory layer that the query service checks for the top results, instead of re-indexing dishes all evening.
Rebuild a city's index from the menus database every night into a new copy, then switch to it, so small errors don't pile up.
A shard is down: its copy answers. If both are down, return results from the other shards with a note, rather than nothing.
The indexer falls behind: searches still work with slightly old menus; the fast layer still hides sold-out dishes.
Search is down entirely: the app falls back to browsing restaurants near you.
Junior / mid: an inverted index (or a search engine), filters, why LIKE '%…%' doesn't scale.
Senior: query cleaning and synonyms, sharding by city, merging shard results, ranking signals, updates within a minute.
Lead: the fast layer for sold out, nightly rebuilds and switching, partial results when shards fail, measuring relevance.
"Search in Hindi or Marathi script?" Index the script and its transliteration, so "पनीर" and "paneer" find the same dishes.
"How do you know ranking is good?" Track what people click and order after searching; a change that helps should raise orders from the first results.
"Searching across cities?" Rare for delivery; if needed, ask each city's shards and merge, like within a city.
"Why not search the menus database with its own full-text search?" Fine to start; a separate index scales and ranks better without loading the database that takes orders.
"How do you test it?" A set of real queries with the dishes people chose, checked after every ranking or synonym change.

body.x: Search is read far more than it's written, so it's served from its own index, never the database. The read-heavy challenge practises the same idea.
